section_summaries.epidemiology: Onchocerciasis, or "river blindness," was first described in 1875 and remains a leading cause of debilitating skin and ocular disease in endemic regions of Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Approximately 37 million people are infected, with 500,000 suffering visual loss, half of whom are blind, and 85.6 million at risk. It is most prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa, where it is endemic in 31 countries, accounting for over 95% of its geographic distribution. Limited transmission persists in Yemen, Venezuela, and Brazil, though successful elimination campaigns have occurred in other Latin American countries. Epidemiologically, foci are classified as hyperendemic (>60% prevalence), mesoendemic (30-60%), and hypoendemic (<30%). In highly endemic areas, O. volvulus infection is acquired early, with over 90% of inhabitants infected by age 20. Increased global migration and travel contribute to more diagnoses in non-endemic areas.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Infectious O. volvulus L3 larvae are transmitted by Simulium black flies and mature into adult worms found in subcutaneous fibrous nodules or onchocercomata. Female worms release thousands of microfilariae into surrounding tissues, which can be ingested by feeding black flies to complete the life cycle. The period from an infective bite to detectable microfilariae in skin is 10 to 20 months. Disease pathology, primarily affecting the skin, lymph nodes, and eyes, results from inflammatory reactions following microfilariae death, secretion of toxic products by granulocytes, deposition of immune complexes, or inflammatory mechanisms induced by Wolbachia-derived products. Most clinical manifestations are related to chronic effects of repeated inflammation. Skin disease involves inflammation around skin-dwelling microfilariae, leading to loss of elasticity and early aging. Histologically, microfilariae are seen at the dermo-epidermal junction. Inflammatory changes in the upper dermis include edema and fibrosis. Ocular lesions result from microfilarial invasion and local death; microfilariae can enter the eye via the bulbar conjunctiva, scleral vessels, nerves, or choroidal/ciliary capillaries. Punctate keratitis involves focal accumulations of lymphocytes and eosinophils around degenerating microfilariae. Sclerosing keratitis is a progressive fibrovascular pannus. Posterior chamber lesions include optic atrophy and chorioretinopathy due to inflammatory damage to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris, leading to loss of photoreceptors and neuroretina.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: The most troublesome symptom is itching, with skin changes classified as acute papular onchodermatitis (APOD) presenting as small pruritic papules, and chronic papular onchodermatitis (CPOD) as flat-topped papules. Localized onchodermatitis, also known as 'sowda,' features pruritic, hyperpigmented, hyperkeratotic plaques, often asymmetric, associated with regional lymphadenopathy. Atrophic skin, common in highly endemic areas, shows loss of elasticity and wrinkling, and reduced sweating and hair. Onchocercal depigmentation, or 'leopard skin,' manifests as patches of complete pigment loss, primarily on the anterior lower leg. Rarely, 'hanging groin' or 'adenolymphocele' develops in heavy, long-standing infections. Subcutaneous fibrous nodules (onchocercomata) containing adult worms are typically found in the iliac crest, trochanter, sacrum, upper thorax, and head. Lymph node changes are common, usually slightly enlarged, firm, and non-tender, but clinically silent. Eye disease includes punctate keratitis (fluffy opacities in corneal stroma) which heals without scarring, sclerosing keratitis (progressive scarring of the cornea), and severe anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) potentially leading to posterior synechiae, pupil deformity, secondary cataracts, and glaucoma. Chorioretinitis or chorioretinopathy is slowly progressive, characterized by RPE atrophy and scarring, culminating in optic atrophy. Other complications include low body weight, diffuse musculoskeletal pain, Nakalanga dwarfism, an association with epilepsy (including nodding syndrome), and reproductive abnormalities like secondary amenorrhea and infertility.
section_summaries.diagnosis: A presumptive diagnosis can be made based on exposure history in endemic areas, subcutaneous nodules, and typical skin or ocular signs. Differential diagnosis for early onchodermatitis includes atopic dermatitis, food allergies, contact dermatitis, insect bites, and scabies. Chronic skin lesions must be distinguished from severe chronic eczema, malnutrition, and presbydermia, while 'leopard skin' requires differentiation from vitiligo and leprosy. Definitive diagnosis relies on identifying microfilariae in skin snips or adult worms from excised or aspirated nodules. Skin snips are obtained using a corneoscleral punch or by elevating a skin crease with a needle, then incubated in saline and examined under a dissecting microscope for emergent microfilariae. Ocular microfilariae can be detected via slit lamp examination, especially after patients sit with their head between their legs for 10 minutes. Highly sensitive and specific antibody detection assays and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for onchocercal DNA in skin snips are used in specialized laboratories, particularly for light infections. A rapid point-of-care serologic test (SD Bioline Onchocerciasis IgG4 Rapid Test) is commercially available, though current serologic assays have limited ability to differentiate past from current infection.
section_summaries.treatment: Ivermectin is the primary drug for onchocerciasis, administered as a single 150 µg/kg dose. It is well tolerated and highly efficacious in reducing skin microfilarial numbers. As it has limited effect on adult worms, repeated annual or semi-annual treatments are necessary to suppress microfilarial levels. For persistent pruritus, treatments every 3 months may be needed. Contraindications for ivermectin include children weighing less than 15 kg (or under 5 years), pregnant women, mothers nursing infants during the first week of life, and individuals with impaired blood-brain barriers due to risk of neurological side effects. Ivermectin significantly benefits anterior segment disease, reducing punctate corneal opacities and microfilariae, and improving early iridocyclitis and sclerosing keratitis. Control programs using ivermectin have greatly impacted ocular onchocerciasis and prevented blindness. A mild Mazzotti-like reaction occurs in 10-20% of patients after the first dose, with reduced severity in subsequent treatments. Reactions include worsening rash, edema, and systemic symptoms like fever and musculoskeletal pain. Doxycycline (200 mg daily for 6 weeks), which targets the Wolbachia endosymbiont, inhibits O. volvulus fertility and kills about 50% of adult worms. This macrofilaricidal approach is a treatment option for individuals not in endemic areas. Extreme caution is required if co-infected with Loa loa, as ivermectin can cause severe encephalitis in heavy L. loa infections (>20,000 microfilariae/mL).
section_summaries.prevention: Onchocerciasis control strategies initially aimed to reduce community microfilarial burdens to negligible morbidity, but the current objective is disease elimination. Elimination has been certified in Ecuador, Colombia, Guatemala, and Mexico. In Africa, elimination efforts rely on annual ivermectin distribution, donated by Merck & Co., and are overseen by the Expanded Special Project for Elimination of Neglected Tropical Diseases (ESPEN). Concerns regarding sub-optimal microfilaricidal responses to ivermectin or potential resistance have prompted the search for adjunctive measures to supplement annual ivermectin distribution programs.

tables.title: BOX 116.1 Pediatric Considerations: Patient Evaluation
rows: Children who have not been in endemic areas for long periods have a very low chance of infection.
Infected children generally present with acute manifestations such as acute papular onchodermatitis, punctate keratitis, or a palpable subcutaneous nodule.

tables.title: BOX 116.2 Pediatric Considerations: Treatment
rows: Ivermectin is not approved for use in children weighing less than 15 kg or under the age of 5.
Doxycycline is contraindicated in children aged below 9 years and in pregnant women.
